query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor boron doping in eutectic high-entropy alloys enhances lamellar-boundary cohesion, increasing both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to undoped lamellar-colony alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructure in its as-cast or homogenized condition.
generation.intervention: Add a small amount of boron (on the order of 0.1 at.%–0.5 at.% B) during vacuum arc melting, followed by standard homogenization and aging to promote uniform dissolution and controlled boundary segregation.
generation.conditions: Use typical melt and casting parameters for eutectic HEAs, then apply standard solution treatment and aging protocols to retain well-defined lamellar colonies while allowing controlled boron segregation. Avoid excessively high boron content to prevent coarse boride formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at lamellar interfaces and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron improves boundary cohesion, suppressing microcrack initiation at colony boundaries under tensile stress and thereby providing a dual benefit of higher yield strength and enhanced ductility at ambient temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped lamellar-colony baseline, the boron-doped alloy will exhibit a measurable increase (approximately 10–20%) in yield strength and a modest (approximately 5–10 percentage point) gain in tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Undoped eutectic high-entropy alloy of the same composition and processing history, except without added boron.
generation.boundary: This effect relies on a boron content below the solubility limit that avoids extensive boride precipitation. Excess boron resulting in large brittle borides could negate any strengthening/ductilizing benefit.
generation.uncertainty: Exact boron content for optimal toughness and strength may vary by specific alloy composition. Excessive boron may trigger undesired secondary phases that reintroduce brittleness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys using identical processing, with one set containing a minor boron addition and the other remaining undoped, then perform comparative tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile yield strength and elongation to failure
Fracture surface examination (SEM fractography) for boundary cracking patterns
Microstructural analysis (XRD, TEM/SEM) to confirm boron segregation and identify potential boride formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not exhibit significantly reduced microcrack formation or any net gains in both strength and ductility relative to the undoped baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

chosen.why: A testable hypothesis is that minor boron doping segregates to lamellar boundaries, reducing local brittleness and inhibiting microcrack initiation under tensile load. By improving boundary cohesion, B doping will raise strength while enhancing ductility relative to the undoped lamellar-colony baseline. These benefits depend on maintaining a stable matrix and avoiding excessive brittle boride formation. Prior work on Ni-based alloys shows improved boundary strength with B doping, supporting this approach. A critical experiment entails tensile tests and fracture-surface analyses of both doped and undoped alloys. Failure to observe improved ductility or reduced boundary fracture when B is added would falsify the hypothesis.
